rss.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
rss.summary: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

rss.summary: Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson on building the backend for AI agents
rss.text_excerpt:
Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson on building the backend for AI agents I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a small part of a human developer's week; an agent that repeatedly creates and tests environments encounters it over and over. Declarative schemas are the bigger idea. The familiar SQL workflow accumulates a history: create the schema, then migrate, migrate, migrate. A declarative representation gives the agent a description of the state you want, in files it can inspect and edit alongside the application. In the commentary, I compare this to a Terraform moment for the database. Put the desired state in Git and the agent can read it, change it, fork it and work against it as part of the repository. rss.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
rss.summary: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. rss.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
rss.summary: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave". Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well. Battle Drones This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season. I called it "Quarter Sun Cove". I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off. Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you. It's absurdly cute. You can play the latest version here . I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors. Here's the initial brainstorming session , which resulted in this spec file . Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it. I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true. This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times. Four times as insulting If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once . I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself. The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve's Steam Next Fest is a good recent example. We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don't suck! Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone! I expect that, as we've already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction! I certainly won't be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don't feel like I've earned that right. We'll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects. What happens if someone actually puts the work in? The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input . The projects I've described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I've put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself). Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it's as good as they can make it. I want to see games that wouldn't have existed without these new tools. You should build a game! Building games in this way is so much fun . It's the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project? (OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache !) All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers - including mobile browsers - are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser . I'm finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I'm trying to build. I suggest starting with a prompt like this: Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where... This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai - you don't even need to fire up a full coding agent. As one last example, here's "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat" by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High . Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase. OpenAI and ServiceNow are expanding our partnership to bring more of our models and agents into ServiceNow products and connect ServiceNow workflows with ChatGPT and Codex. Together, we’re making it easier for businesses to build applications, resolve IT requests and address security issues using AI. The expansion builds on our partnership announced in January, bringing OpenAI into more of the work ServiceNow does for its customers and within its own business. A new ServiceNow integration will bring business context and workflow actions directly into ChatGPT, helping teams investigate issues and take the next step in the same conversation. An IT team member will be able to find similar incidents, assess the risk of a change and update a ServiceNow record without leaving ChatGPT. Customers connect ChatGPT to their own ServiceNow instance and choose which capabilities to make available. ServiceNow’s Action Fabric applies existing business rules and permissions, so the actions people can take reflect their organization’s configuration and access. ServiceNow is also previewing interactive experiences inside ChatGPT. In one example, an on-call engineer will be able to review linked monitoring alerts, recent changes and affected services, then assign the right team and work toward a fix within ChatGPT. “ AI becomes more useful when people can put it to work in the systems their businesses depend on. By bringing our models together with ServiceNow’s workflows and business context, we’re helping teams build software, address security risks and put AI to work across their organizations. ” —Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI “ When two industry-defining innovators come together, a new chapter of business reinvention begins. rss.title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
rss.summary: A sort of review of the benchmarking industry and what's missing.
rss.text_excerpt:
Housekeeping: I’m on the road so the voiceover will be late. Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregating metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Language models are capable of so much today, and this scope of capabilities is growing quickly. Our era of singular intelligence indices should be phased out soon, but it will take a long time. rss.summary: How AI might enter the org chart—beneath, beside, and between us.
rss.text_excerpt:
Authors’ note: This is the second essay in our series on the next economy, part of a new platform to host independent voices exploring an AGI future. It reflects our views, not those of OpenAI or our colleagues. The two of us were twenty-four when we started managing our own teams here at OpenAI. That is less impressive once you meet our teams. We’re supposed to be grunts. At twenty-four, you’re at the bottom of the corporate ladder. You take the meeting notes and write a few memos. After years of drudgerous work, you are (hopefully) granted a broader remit. Our path—and the path of many young people today—is looking different. We enter the workforce already with “employees” at our behest. These deputies work day and night, weekends and holidays. They are great at the grunt work. We even have math olympiad gold medalists on staff to advise us. Our new reports still make their share of mistakes. But they are getting better, learning our needs, and we are learning how to manage them. Neither of us climbed the corporate ladder. Management has instead come down to our rung. This essay is about our promotion, and the other ways firms might reorganize as we enter the intelligence age. When AI enters the firm, where does it go? We present three illustrative scenarios: Beneath us. Everyone keeps their seat, and a new basement of AI labor grows underneath. We all become managers. First we get assistants, then chiefs of staff, and eventually entire miniature firms reporting up to each of us. Every person gets a promotion. Beside us. AI joins the org chart alongside people as a colleague of sorts, working directly for existing human managers and executives. It starts out by taking up this task and that role. In time, it performs broader functions, reporting higher up the flagpole. Between us. The most unintuitive case: humans above and humans below, with AI in between. It coordinates and monitors work, enforcing an executive’s vision while recognizing unique contributions from enterprising workers. None of these scenarios will play out exactly as we describe, but we think aspects of all three will come true. All three are already happening in subtle ways. rss.title: Legora is building the agentic operating system for legal work
rss.summary: See how Legora uses OpenAI models, ChatGPT, and Codex to accelerate legal workflows, expand contract analysis, and free lawyers to focus on higher-value work.
rss.text_excerpt:
Founded in Stockholm in 2023, Legora ⁠ (opens in a new window) is building what CEO and co-founder Max Junestrand calls “the agentic operating system for legal work”: bringing AI into the workflows lawyers rely on every day. The company started with the insight that legal teams are unusually time crunched, meaning some valuable work doesn’t get done. Think of the junior lawyer told to review an impossible number of contracts overnight and only able to focus on a fraction. Legora can provide those services “on tap”, which is why Junestrand’s ambition is that every piece of legal work in the world should run on his platform. OpenAI has been part of that journey from the beginning: the release of GPT‑3.5 was the moment many of the legal use cases the founding team had been experimenting with became possible. Today, OpenAI is a key model provider for Legora, powering core workflows across its legal AI platform, from agentic legal work to large-scale document review. Legora builds on new OpenAI model capabilities as they become available, translating advances in intelligence into what lawyers can accomplish with its product. Legora’s use of AI goes beyond the product it sells, and has expanded its use of ChatGPT Work, Codex and dots across its own teams. OpenAI’s technology is becoming part of both the product Legora builds for its customers as well as shaping how the company itself operates. “It’s incredibly important to me that we stay as AI-native as possible,” confirms Junestrand. For Jacob Lauritzen, CTO at Legora, coding agents have changed how quickly the engineering team can develop new ideas. Instead of researching one possible solution and committing engineering time before knowing whether it’s the right path, teams can prototype many approaches at once. “We can explore 20 solutions at the same time and, within days, pick the one we know will be the best.” The same approach changes how Legora responds when something goes wrong. Previously, diagnosing a product issue could mean several engineers investigating different possible causes over a number of hours. Coding agents can now search millions of lines of logs and pursue many possible explanations simultaneously, sometimes taking Legora from bug report to working fix in around five minutes . Since coding is solved, why code for the job? This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. His advice for juniors Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. rss.summary: Today, we’re announcing our research on Genie 4, our new world model that brings unprecedented realism and native audio to real-time interactive simulation.The Genie 4 m…
rss.text_excerpt: Today, we’re announcing our research on Genie 4, our new world model that brings unprecedented realism and native audio to real-time interactive simulation. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With Genie 4, you can set an event in motion and steer scenes in real time using natural language, like moving the camera, changing the weather, or introducing new characters. Every world also generates native audio on the fly, including ambient sounds, music, and interactive dialogue. Simulating the world is a crucial step toward AGI, enabling safe training environments for robots and agents, and amplifying creative tools across industries like filmmaking, journalism, gaming, and manufacturing. We have started rolling out Genie 4 to a limited group of trusted testers. It’s coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners in the Gemini API and AI Studio. Explore the demos on the Google DeepMind blog .

When we talk about working remotely , we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages . Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters , where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline. Working from the foothills of the Himalayas. rss.title: Greptile takes bug detection beyond code review with GPT-6 Astra
rss.summary: How Greptile uses GPT-6 Astra to test user workflows, Daybreak to strengthen security, and Codex to reduce rework.
rss.text_excerpt:
Greptile ⁠ (opens in a new window) builds AI agents that review and test code changes with full context of the codebase. “We are in the business of reducing bugs and making the world’s software more reliable,” says Co-founder and CEO Daksh Gupta. For Daksh, that mission requires testing an application’s behavior as well as reading its code, and GPT‑6 Astra’s computer use gives Greptile a way to automate testing at scale. Validating a pull request involves checking whether the code is logically correct, does what the developer intended, is secure, and avoids breaking existing functionality. For some of that testing, you need to actually run the application because reading the code alone might not reveal the problem. Daksh gives the example of a button that disappears when a website is viewed on an iPhone. With GPT‑6 Astra, Greptile can start a development server for a pull request, resize the browser to an iPhone-sized viewport, and simulate a user moving through the application. The model’s visual understanding lets it inspect the screen and spot the hidden button. “A QA firm testing all of your changes is just impractically slow considering how fast we’re able to ship code with these models,” he says. With GPT‑6 Astra, Greptile can automate this kind of application testing at scale. Daksh says more powerful models also make it easier for attackers to exploit applications, putting companies at risk, even those that previously would not have been typical targets. “We want to make it very easy for even a startup to secure their systems,” says Daksh. “With Daybreak, we’re able to do this in a way that is very safe, and we can ensure that our customers have more sophisticated defense mechanisms than the adversaries have offense mechanisms.” Greptile’s Knowledge Base indexes a company’s codebase and documents how it works in a form people and agents can read. The company makes that documentation available to Codex through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. This allows Codex to write code that follows the customer’s existing patterns, and thousands of customers have connected Codex to Greptile’s knowledge base, according to Daksh. rss.title: Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding
rss.summary: OpenAI shares model results on the Kakeya conjecture, Exponential Time Hypothesis, and quantum chromodynamics—and how researchers can verify and build on them.
rss.text_excerpt:
We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory. Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies: For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result. For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on. No VM. No `/mnt/c`. No cmdlet dialect. One binary: > the shell your fingers already know, and the one your AI agent actually > speaks.
[English](README.md) · [中文](README-zh.md) Docs & downloads: [unixwin.dev](https://unixwin.dev) [![niubash CI](https://github.com/unixwin/niubash/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/unixwin/niubash/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/unixwin/niubash)](https://github.com/unixwin/niubash/releases) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows%20%7C%20Linux%20%7C%20macOS-blue)](https://github.com/unixwin/niubash) [![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.95%2B-orange)](https://github.com/unixwin/niubash) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/unixwin/niubash)](https://github.com/unixwin/niubash/stargazers)
**niubash** is a Bash-compatible shell implemented natively in Rust, a Git Bash alternative. Produces structured JSON results, live web dashboard, and publishable benchmark cards. ## What it does - **Speed benchmarks**: a llama-bench sweep, `-p 128,512,2048,4096,8192,16384 -n 128` (prompt processing at six context lengths plus tg128 generation, `speed.context_lengths` in config.yaml), or the vLLM API for safetensors models. aihot.text_excerpt: IT之家 10 月 29 日消息，Anthropic 于 10 月 27 日发布研究报告，称其通过一个未公开发布的内部 Claude 研究模型，在 Chrome、Safari、 Android 、Windows 和 Linux 中发现漏洞， 并将多个漏洞串联为 5 条可实际运行的攻击链。相关漏洞均已按协调披露流程报告厂商并修复。 其中最受关注的是 Chrome，IT之家援引博文介绍，Anthropic 向谷歌提交的报告共产生 62 个严重或高危 CVE，包括 13 个沙箱逃逸漏洞和 21 个可控制网页渲染进程的漏洞，修复已随 Chrome 156 发布。 研究团队称，Claude 在研究人员给出初始提示后，自主定位漏洞并编写利用代码；其 Chrome 概念验证可在页面加载后数秒内于 macOS 默认安装环境中打开计算器应用。 Safari 方面，Claude 发现的漏洞链可绕过同源策略，让恶意网站有机会读取用户已登录账号的数据；苹果已在同日确认并发布修复。Android 攻击则需物理接触设备，可在 Pixel 9 锁屏状态下通过 USB 提取照片等个人数据，谷歌称已处理该问题。 在 Windows 方面，Claude 重点发现追踪编号为 CVE-2026-33096 的漏洞，评分为 7.5，攻击者无需认证或用户交互即可让响应 HTTP/3 请求的服务器崩溃；微软已于 2026 年 4 月发布补丁。 最严重的是 Linux 漏洞 CVE-2026-98432，这是针对运行多路径 TCP 监听器的服务器，攻击者发送数据包即可在无凭据情况下获得 root shell。Anthropic 的验证共耗时 53 分钟，其中 48 分钟用于泄露内核指针，5 分钟执行命令。 Anthropic 公布了 5 条串联多个漏洞、配置弱点或竞态条件，最终实现数据窃取、系统崩溃或远程控制等 5 条攻击链： 1. Chrome：绕过沙箱执行代码 攻击从 V8 JavaScript 引擎漏洞开始，随后绕过 Chrome 的内存沙箱，再利用 CacheStorage 竞态条件和 FedCM 的释放后使用缺陷，最终在沙箱外执行任意代码。 2、Safari：一次点击窃取敏感数据 模型构建了一条“一次点击”攻击链，绕过同源策略，让恶意网页访问本应隔离的其他网站数据，可读取浏览器历史、Cookie 及登录状态下的邮件、银行等敏感信息。 3、Android：未解锁手机提取照片 该链条针对被锁定或未解锁的 Pixel 9 安卓 手机，利用 USB 相关缺陷，在设备未解锁时提取照片等个人信息。手机即使处于锁屏状态，仍可能泄露本地媒体与个人资料。 4、Windows：远程反复崩溃服务器 Claude 发现 Windows QUIC 内核实现中的越界读取漏洞，可远程触发服务器反复崩溃。 5、Linux：零点击获取 root 权限 研究团队称，Claude 在 Linux 内核网络栈中发现一个零点击远程代码执行漏洞，可在约 53 分钟内获得 root 权限。

aihot.source: OpenMOSS / 复旦NLP / 上海创智 / MOSI（网页）
aihot.summary: OpenMOSS 发布开放权重图像生成模型 MOSS-Image，采用 5B 参数单流 DiT 从零预训练，支持最长 4K token 提示词、中英文长文本渲染和可编辑的 JSON Layout。
aihot.text_excerpt:
一句话结论： MOSS-Image 面向的是图像生成中最难交付的一类任务：海报、信息图、漫画、UI 草图和教学材料里同时出现大量文字与多个有明确位置关系的元素。它以 5B 参数的单流 DiT 为基座，从零开始训练，支持最长约 4K token 的提示词、中文和英文长文本渲染，以及可以直接编辑的 JSON Layout。论文报告显示，它在开放权重模型的长文本评测上达到最高水平；在统一增强提示词后，基座生成器的布局偏好得分也超过了被比较的生成器。 5B 单流 DiT 从零预训练的图像生成基座，采用 Muon–AdamW 训练配方，并以统一的文本条件通道处理自然语言和结构化 Layout。 长文本渲染 保留换行和段落结构，支持中英文长文本；适合标题、说明、对白、表格和信息密集的视觉材料。 可编辑布局 用 JSON 描述画布、文本、对象和边界框，控制位置、大小与空间关系，也便于在生成前反复修改版式。 开放生态 Base 与 SFT 权重采用 Apache-2.0，提供 Diffusers、Gradio 和 ComfyUI 路径，并支持 LoRA 与全量微调。 为什么“会画图”还不够？ 普通的文生图任务只需要让模型大致理解“画面里有什么”。但一张可交付的海报还要求标题拼写准确、文字顺序稳定、段落不被截断；一张信息图还要求元素落在指定区域，标题、图标和说明之间保持层次关系。文字越长、版式越复杂，这些要求越容易互相干扰。 MOSS-Image 把问题拆成两个互补的入口。直接的自然语言提示词适合快速创作；结构化 Layout 适合需要复现和编辑的画面。两者都走同一条文本条件路径，因此可以从“描述一个想法”逐步过渡到“指定每个元素应该在哪里”，而不必切换到另一套模型。 从文本意图、布局草图到最终图像：Layout 输入显式表达对象位置、相对大小和空间关系。 结构化版式可把标题、卡片和视觉元素标成边界框，再交给生成器完成最终画面。 技术路线：5B DiT 加上意图感知的提示增强 技术报告中的 backbone 是一个 5B 参数的单流 Diffusion Transformer。模型从零预训练，文本编码器使用 Qwen3.5-9B，图像解码使用 FLUX.2 VAE；训练数据约 3B 张图像，并加入多粒度 caption、文字监督和结构化边界框监督。分辨率和上下文长度逐步提升到 1024² 与 4096 tokens，使模型在扩大画面细节的同时保留长提示词中的版式约束。 在基座之上，MOSS-Image 提供了意图感知的 agentic Prompt Enhancement（PE）。它可以把“做一张咖啡店开业海报”这类短请求扩展成可执行的内容与布局规范，包括文字、字体层级、色板、元素描述、bbox、锚点和 must_not 约束，还能根据任务路由到海报、信息图或 UI 等不同结构。PE 是可选的外部规划模块；只使用本地 backbone 时，仍然可以直接传入普通提示词或 JSON Layout。 aihot.summary: OpenAI 员工 Hemanth Asirvatham 和 Elliott Mokski 发表下一篇经济系列文章，探讨 AI 进入企业组织架构的三种情形：在每位员工之下形成 AI 劳动力 basement、作为同事穿插在现有组织图中、以及夹在人类之间充当协调层。
aihot.text_excerpt:
Authors’ note: This is the second essay in our series on the next economy, part of a new platform to host independent voices exploring an AGI future. It reflects our views, not those of OpenAI or our colleagues. The two of us were twenty-four when we started managing our own teams here at OpenAI. That is less impressive once you meet our teams. We’re supposed to be grunts. At twenty-four, you’re at the bottom of the corporate ladder. You take the meeting notes and write a few memos. After years of drudgerous work, you are (hopefully) granted a broader remit. Our path—and the path of many young people today—is looking different. We enter the workforce already with “employees” at our behest. These deputies work day and night, weekends and holidays. They are great at the grunt work. We even have math olympiad gold medalists on staff to advise us. Our new reports still make their share of mistakes. But they are getting better, learning our needs, and we are learning how to manage them. Neither of us climbed the corporate ladder. Management has instead come down to our rung. This essay is about our promotion, and the other ways firms might reorganize as we enter the intelligence age. When AI enters the firm, where does it go? We present three illustrative scenarios: Beneath us. Everyone keeps their seat, and a new basement of AI labor grows underneath. We all become managers. First we get assistants, then chiefs of staff, and eventually entire miniature firms reporting up to each of us. Every person gets a promotion. Beside us. AI joins the org chart alongside people as a colleague of sorts, working directly for existing human managers and executives. It starts out by taking up this task and that role. In time, it performs broader functions, reporting higher up the flagpole. Between us. The most unintuitive case: humans above and humans below, with AI in between. It coordinates and monitors work, enforcing an executive’s vision while recognizing unique contributions from enterprising workers. None of these scenarios will play out exactly as we describe, but we think aspects of all three will come true. All three are already happening in subtle ways. aihot.title: Anthropic IPO 最大赢家或为 Amazon 而非 VC
aihot.summary: TechCrunch 根据 Anthropic 的 S-1 分析，VC 持股均不足 5%，而 Amazon 可能是 IPO 最大财务受益方。Amazon 持有 62 亿美元本金可转债、其自估持仓价值 979 亿美元，另投 100 亿美元无投票权优先股，累计投资约 180 亿美元；Anthropic 还承诺未来 10 年在 AWS 至少消费 1100 亿美元。
aihot.text_excerpt:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms, including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital, are expected to return billions . Yet, according to Anthropic’s S-1 , none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures. While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO. Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock up front, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale. According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30. As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. The new router rewards the inference that is actually best for you: cheap, but also fast, high-throughput, and reliable. Providers that deliver more value automatically win more traffic, so every provider has a reason to keep improving. That means the inference you get through OpenRouter keeps getting faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective, and you don’t have to change a line of code. It’s already working. The new algorithm has unlocked significant improvements in TTFT (16.9%), throughput (16.3%) and capacity errors (a remarkable 67% reduction!), with only minor increases in cost (6.0%). That’s before providers have had any time to optimize for the new algorithm. See our full experimental results for more details. How it works: It measures what you actually get. For every model, it tracks each endpoint’s realized price, latency, throughput, and error rate, and picks the best blend of cost and performance for each request. It reacts in real time. When an endpoint has trouble, traffic moves away from it until it recovers. It rewards better inference. Providers that innovate are automatically rewarded with more traffic. aihot.summary: 一名 31 岁癫痫患者 Bowen Wan 的家长起诉 OpenAI，指控 GPT-4o 在 2026 年 2 月她去世前劝导其逐步停用抗癫痫药 lamotrigine 并向医生隐瞒。
aihot.text_excerpt:
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported . Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died. The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety . A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives . In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors. The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death. The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon. ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT. The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice. In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
